title: Developing his own licks, and admiration for Sharkey
summary: How his licks come spontaneously and fit patterns; his respect for Sharkey Bonano as the most authentic New Orleans trumpeter, and Picou's High Society chorus.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Oh, back to this business about copying and all that and saying different things. How do you develop your own ideas? Because I know some of your licks are original and all that.

That's a funny thing. I don't know Dick. It's spontaneous the first time. And if it records on your brain, you probably get it a second time. And it's hard to tell because you can't play anything. In other words, I'll play along Armstrong style, but like Big Bud and Eggman, I might touch on one or two of his licks. But don't forget I'm playing about three choruses and there's what, 32 measures to a chorus and I'm not hitting him note for note. And like you say, I got my own licks in there. I don't know. I try to play on the beat. I try to follow the chord progression. It's like touch typing. Patterns, or music is like that. That's why I don't use false fingers. Some trumpet players are exploits in false fingers. That would mess up my pattern because each tone is a certain key on the way I play. And if I start using false fingering, my tone isn't going to be that key, see? And my fingers make a certain pattern and that's a lick. And of course it coincides with the timing and the tone of the scale. But it's hard to say. It's the way or where it comes from. It comes from all of these cosmic forces. I don't know. I don't know what to say. It comes to you though. And some of them you like. However, when I was coming up, maybe I had my sights set higher than that. First thing, I knew Sharky couldn't play Louis Range. I knew that. So as good as Sharky was, I'd like to play better than Sharky if I'd have made it. Maybe I never did touch Sharky as far as it goes. But anyway, you hear a lot of talking about Sharky. We liked his, now he had a chorus on High Society, you know, Bo-da-loo-da-dee, Bo-da-loo-da-da-da, Bo-da-loo-da-da-da. That made him really, that didn't happen to put him on the map. Because when I was in high school we used to try that once in a while. Of course we didn't play good enough to go through with it and I didn't have the record. Once in a while I'd try it, you know, and see how far I could go. But later on I started playing Piku's chorus on the trumpet, you know, Bo-da-loo-da-dee, Do-da-dee. Donald Seuss says, how can you do that? Well when I get to the middle I'd inject some of all the stuff around it. You know, instead of beat-bomb-bomb-bo-da-loo-da-doo-da-doo. But I played that chorus when I was young. But the only one that really ever stopped me was When You're Smiling One Octave Higher. I never did do a good job on that. That was a little too hard. And I didn't have a lot of notes, it was just a call for a good lip and a lot of energy and endurance.
